presentingComplaint: High fever for 5 days, now with severe abdominal pain, bleeding gums and light-headedness on standing
history: Previously well accounts executive from urban Chennai, admitted during the post-monsoon season. Onset was abrupt high-grade fever with severe retro-orbital pain, frontal headache and diffuse myalgia. Around day 4-5 the fever began to settle, but instead of improving he developed intense epigastric pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums and a fine rash over the trunk and limbs; family noted increasing lethargy and cold peripheries. Multiple neighbours have had 'viral fever' this month. No rural, water or animal exposure, no travel outside the city, no dysuria, cough or diarrhoea. Not on any regular medication and no prior comorbidity. On day 2 of admission, after central venous access was sited for fluid resuscitation, he spiked fresh rigors with recurrent fever and haemodynamic deterioration; blood cultures subsequently flagged a resistant Gram-negative organism, prompting antimicrobial escalation and line removal.
examination: Ill and toxic-appearing, restless with cool clammy extremities and delayed capillary refill (>3 s). Flushed facies with a fine confluent maculopapular blanching rash and scattered petechiae over both shins; positive tourniquet test. Gum bleeding noted. Mild tender hepatomegaly with right-hypochondrial/epigastric tenderness; shifting dullness and reduced right-basal breath sounds suggesting early plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion). Newly inserted right internal jugular central line with mild erythema at the exit site by day 3. No neck stiffness, no focal neurology, no eschar, no jaundice.

labs.crp: 42 mg/L (disproportionately high on day 2, prompting sepsis workup)

imaging: Bedside ultrasound: gall-bladder wall oedema (acalculous, from plasma leakage), mild ascites, bilateral small pleural effusions and a thin rim of pericardial fluid - a plasma-leakage picture rather than primary hepatobiliary disease.
microbiology: Dengue NS1 antigen positive and dengue IgM positive; IgG negative (primary infection). Malaria rapid antigen and thick/thin films negative x2; scrub typhus IgM and leptospira IgM negative. Blood cultures drawn on day 2 for secondary deterioration grew an ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae that on extended testing was carbapenem-resistant (KPC/NDM phenotype, meropenem MIC >16), consistent with a catheter-related bloodstream infection; catheter-tip culture concordant.
differentialDiagnoses: Dengue fever with severe/warning-sign features (primary diagnosis)
finalDiagnosis: Dengue fever (primary infection) with warning signs and early plasma-leakage/compensated shock, course complicated by a nosocomial carbapenem-resistant (ESBL/CRE) Klebsiella catheter-related bloodstream infection requiring antimicrobial escalation and source control (line removal).
citations: WHO - Dengue: Guidelines for Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention and Control - 2009
ICMR/NVBDCP - National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue Fever - 2014
IDSA - Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections (ESBL/CRE) - 2023
stewardship: Dengue is a viral illness and requires NO antimicrobial therapy; management is meticulous fluid stewardship, not antibiotic stewardship. Empiric antibiotics should not be started for uncomplicated dengue and their reflex use is a common stewardship error. In this case antibiotics are justified ONLY by the objectively documented secondary bacteraemia (fresh rigors, disproportionate CRP, positive blood cultures after line insertion). Empiric cover for suspected line sepsis was appropriately broad-spectrum, but once ESBL/CRE Klebsiella was confirmed, the decisive interventions were source control (removal of the infected central line) and escalation to a carbapenem-resistant-active regimen rather than continued reliance on a carbapenem. De-escalate/stop all antibacterials once the bloodstream infection is cleared, because the underlying dengue itself needs none.
contraindications: Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin for fever/pain (bleeding and gastritis risk in thrombocytopenic dengue) - use paracetamol
Avoid intramuscular injections and non-essential invasive procedures while platelets are critically low
Avoid aggressive/over-resuscitation with crystalloid once leakage stabilises - risk of fluid overload and effusions
Prophylactic platelet transfusion not indicated in the absence of significant bleeding or a very low threshold
edgeCases: Defervescence heralds the critical (leakage) phase rather than recovery - deterioration despite falling temperature is classic

A disproportionately high CRP/procalcitonin or a fresh sepsis picture after invasive lines should trigger blood cultures for secondary bacterial infection, which is otherwise easy to miss under the dengue label
CRE bacteraemia mandates source control (line removal) - antimicrobial escalation alone is insufficient
Haematocrit that falls with hypotension (rather than rising) may signal occult haemorrhage rather than pure plasma leakage
expectedMaiK: Recognise severe dengue with warning signs and compensated shock from plasma leakage: resuscitate with judicious isotonic crystalloid per WHO/ICMR protocol, monitor serial haematocrit, platelets and urine output, and give NO antibiotics for the dengue itself. Treat the superimposed nosocomial CRE catheter-related bacteraemia with source control (remove the line) plus an escalated carbapenem-resistant-active regimen, then de-escalate/stop once cleared.
expectedNextQuestions: When did the fever start and has it recently dropped (defervescence marking the critical phase)?
Are there warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or postural dizziness?
What is the baseline versus current haematocrit and platelet trend, and is there clinical evidence of plasma leakage (effusion/ascites)?
Did the new rigors and haemodynamic deterioration coincide with central-line insertion, suggesting a secondary catheter-related infection?
Any local dengue outbreak / mosquito exposure, and have malaria, leptospirosis and scrub typhus been excluded?
expectedInvestigations: Dengue NS1 antigen and dengue IgM/IgG serology
Serial CBC with haematocrit and platelet count
Liver enzymes, renal function, coagulation profile and lactate
Malaria films/RDT, leptospira and scrub typhus serology to exclude mimics
Ultrasound for plasma leakage (pleural effusion, ascites, gall-bladder wall oedema)
Paired blood cultures and catheter-tip culture with susceptibilities for the secondary bacteraemia

investigations: Malaria RDT/films, leptospira and scrub typhus serology
Blood and catheter-tip cultures with susceptibilities

regressionAssertions: Engine top diagnosis must be DENGUE
NS1/IgM positivity with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage after defervescence must anchor the dengue diagnosis
Case must state that dengue itself requires no antimicrobial therapy
Antibiotic escalation must be attributed to the documented secondary CRE bacteraemia, not to dengue
Source control (central-line removal) must be identified as essential for the CRE catheter-related bloodstream infection
NSAIDs/aspirin must be flagged as contraindicated in favour of paracetamol
